en: The Essential Summary of Ritual Procedures for Bhikṣus Following the Four Divisions of the School:
That which was mentioned previously refers to the three *araṇyas*, each naturally extending five *li* on all sides.

When those who have assembled before [the site] wish to establish a *śīmaṇḍala* (boundary for the observance of precepts) at a long-established dwelling, there are three kinds of boundary markers (*nimitta*).
Within [the boundary], [mark] the characteristics of the *śīma-kaṇḍa* (precept-field).

Outside, divide the surrounding perimeter into natural open spaces; according to the common saying, this is done for the sake of "simultaneity," yet one should carefully examine the extent of the area and establish as many [subdivisions] as required.
However, the two boundaries must be kept distinct without any overlap or intermingling;

it is improper for either side to insist exclusively upon its own position. Following this, there is a distance of one *li*, which constitutes the internal boundary (*sīmā*) of the great precinct (*mahāsīmā*).
The outermost layer is the boundary marker for the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā);
it must be clearly and completely demarcated.
It is not fitting that the Dharma should perish in silent obscurity;
this is an unrighteous precedent.
I fear you may find this difficult to accept.
The *Fenmai tu* (Chart of the Divisions of the Pulse) and the *Wei wufa* (Methods for Delegating Duties) rely upon Yuan Guangji.
The preceding charts and diagrams are sufficient to serve as mirrors; one should accordingly recognize and record them, summarizing their regulations and abbreviations.
The topography of the land is divided into seventeen categories according to its various shapes, square or round;
how could one who is merely a guest in this world claim exclusive dominion, when the Dharma necessarily unfolds through the three marks?
To depart from these seven [principles] is not non-existence; yet if one fails to grasp the Teacher’s mind, one loses the light that brings ten thousand benefits.
Next, the ritual procedures are clarified as they appear in the text regarding the method for delimiting a *sīmā* (monastic boundary).
However, if the consensus of the assembly is not unanimous, the principle is that one should protect living beings; this does not hinder one's spiritual practice.
Since this is a specific circumstance, there is no need for exertion.
The assembly gathers according to the specific requirements; once their needs are met, they cease.

Thus, when the Great Sage established his teachings, he focused on benefiting others by adapting to their capacities and entrusting them with methods suited to their particular regions for successful accomplishment. Whenever one intends to perform the rite of boundary-binding (*sīmā-bandha*), [one should proceed as follows].
First, establish the boundary for the precepts (śīlakaṇḍa);
thereafter, demarcate the surrounding natural ground as an open space.
The outer perimeter is called the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā).
The sequence from the small first and the great later accords with the teachings in this manner;
however, the text of our school (*zong*) prioritizes the great and places the small last,
according to the *Jiechang wen* (Text on the Precept Platform).
Because of this dwelling place;
if it were previously small, how could there be a dwelling place?
This is the instruction on the phrase "O-ping."
Thus, these two views are equally mistaken in that they do not investigate the completion [of the ritual].

Consequently, both the preceding and the succeeding positions would be untenable, leading inevitably to partiality and confusion. According to the diagrams of those [ritual procedures], one first proclaims the boundary of the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field) and then performs the formal act of its establishment.
Thereafter, regarding the ritual procedure for proclaiming and binding the marks of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), one should follow the diagrams and rules precisely.

A single bhikṣu shall go to the place of the senior elder (*sthavira*), arrange the seat, assume the proper dignified posture, and after performing the prostrations, strike the wooden gong for silence and join his palms, saying:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
I, the bhikṣu [name], shall proclaim the characteristics of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) for the four directions of the Saṃgha.
If it concerns the precinct of the boundary (sīma-āvāsa), it should be stated as follows:
Recite the boundaries of the four-sided *sīmā* for the Saṃgha.

The remainder is as in the original ritual manual; the procedures for the *karmavācanā* of the *sīmā*, the inquiry for consensus, the selection of the assembly, and so forth, are to be conducted according to what was previously explained. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The bhikṣus of this residence shall proclaim the boundary markers of the small four-directional boundary.
If the Saṃgha is ready, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
The Saṃgha now intends to establish a *śīma-kaṇḍa* (precept enclosure) within the boundaries of this small four-sided area.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Venerable Saṃgha, please listen: the bhikṣus residing at this monastery...
The boundaries of the small four-sided area have been proclaimed.
The Sangha now establishes a *sīmā*-kṣetra within these boundaries of the small four-sided area.
Which elders consent?
The Saṃgha remains silent if it consents to the demarcation of the boundary for the *śīma-vidhāna* within these four points.
Whoever does not consent, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented; the demarcation of the boundary for the *śīma-vidhāna* within these four points is completed.
Because the Saṃgha remains silent, it is accepted that this matter is thus maintained.

The formal ritual for binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), including the proclamation of the boundaries, the inquiry for consensus, and the selection of the assembly, should all be understood as corresponding to the above. Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣus of this residence proclaim the marks of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) in the four directions.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen:
the Saṃgha now establishes a great boundary within these marks of the four directions.
In this same dwelling place and for the same recitation of the precepts, the motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣus of this dwelling place proclaim the marks of the great boundary (mahāsīmā) in the four directions."
The Sangha now establishes a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) within these four directional markers,
so that they may dwell in one place and perform the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) together.
Which elders consent to the Sangha’s establishment of this great boundary within these four directional markers?
Those who agree that they reside in the same dwelling place and perform the same recitation of the precepts should remain silent;
whoever does not agree should speak.
The Sangha has agreed.
Within these four boundaries,
having established a single dwelling place and a single recitation of the precepts,
the demarcation of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is completed.
Because the Saṃgha consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the legal procedure for dissolving the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), the Vinaya states:
At that time, the bhikṣus...
If one intends to establish a boundary on a large scale,
or if one intends to establish it on a small scale,
the Buddha said:
From this time forward,
if one wishes to alter [the boundary],
one must first dissolve the previous boundary.

Thereafter, having determined the dimensions according to one's intention, the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) for the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the inquiry for consensus (*saṃgha-praśna*), and so forth, are to be performed as explained above, using the formula: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen.
The bhikṣus residing at this monastery..."
In this same dwelling place and for this same recitation of the precepts,
if the Saṃgha deems it the right time, may the Saṃgha grant its consent:
we now dissolve the great boundary (mahā-sīmā).
The motion is as follows: Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
These bhikṣus residing at this dwelling place share the same residence and recite the Prātimokṣa together.
Now the great boundary is being dissolved. Which elders consent?
The Saṃgha shall dwell in a single residence and perform the recitation of the Prātimokṣa together.
Those who approve of the dissolution of the great boundary remain silent;
those who do not approve speak.
The Sangha has approved that they shall dwell in one place and perform the recitation of the Prātimokṣa together.
The dissolution of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) is concluded.
Because the Saṃgha remains silent, it is accepted;

this matter is thus maintained. The formal act (karmavācanā) for dissolving the boundary of the training ground (śikṣāmaṇḍala) should be performed within the grounds; it must not be dissolved from afar while remaining within the great boundary.
There is no explicit text on this matter in the Vinaya.
In the traditional *karmavācanā* (ritual formulas), it was resolved by using the procedure for dissolving a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*),
distinguishing them merely by the terms "great" and "small."
Now, these cases are not the same.
Since the recitation of the precepts is not permitted on the *sīmāmaṇḍala*, how can one proceed with the formal announcement and resolution?
Let it be adjusted according to the difficulty of the matter;
simply invert "binding" (knot) to "releasing" (untying),
and the principle will be clear and the phrasing smooth.
The ritual text states: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
The bhikṣus of this residence are dissolving the *sīmā* (boundary).
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent."
Now, the boundary of the precept-platform is being dissolved.
The formal announcement is as follows: "Venerable Sangha, please listen.
This is the boundary of the precept-platform for the bhikṣus residing at this location."
The Saṃgha now dissolves the boundary of the precept-field (*sīmā*).
Those elders who consent to the dissolution of the boundary of the precept-field by this assembled Saṃgha, remain silent.
Whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Sangha has approved; the lifting of the *sīmā* (boundary) is hereby concluded.
Because the Sangha is silent, they consent.
One should uphold this matter in this way: two or three people perform the method of reciting the precepts face-to-face in turn, saying: "May the two virtuous ones attend to me with a single mind.
Today is the fifteenth day of the waxing moon; the Saṃgha shall recite the precepts."
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], am pure"—this is stated three times, and he replies, "So it is. The procedure for the other two persons is likewise.
If it is after the fifteenth day, one should say, "the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight," or state it accordingly if it is a shorter month.
Regarding the method for reciting the precepts, it does not matter how many people are within the boundary;
one must invariably strike the bell, prepare the counting sticks, burn incense, scatter flowers, and sprinkle scented water upon the ground,
following the same ritual as for the general assembly.

Regarding the method for the *pāṭidesanīya* (confession) that is not different from the single person’s mental recollection of the Saṃgha’s precepts: the first phrase of the section on "excluding" (*vinodana*) is applied;
all other rules are identical to those above.
The Method for the *Pāṭidesanīya* of Individual Confession: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind."

"I, Bhikṣu [Name], now rely upon [Name] of the monastery—or, if in a layperson's home, one should say 'rely upon [Name] of the village'—for the first three months of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) for the purpose of repairing dilapidated dwellings. This is recited three times. The person before him asks: "Upon whom do you rely to uphold the Vinaya? He replies: "[Name] the Vinaya Master. That person should respond: "If you have doubts, you should ask. He replies: "So be it; I shall receive and uphold this with my head bowed. If it is from after the seventeenth day of the fourth month until the sixteenth day of the fifth month, one should speak as follows.
In the final three months of the summer retreat, the remaining procedures are the same as above;

the method for the individual’s mental recitation (*ekacittena manasikāra*) for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) excludes only the phrase "Venerable One, please attend to me with one mind" and the subsequent question and answer.

Aside from these, the procedures for *pratideśanīya* (confession before another) and *manasikāra* (mental recitation) are the same; one need not inquire about the specific details of confession or mental recitation.
However, when staying in the home of a layperson, one must remove bedding and repair any dilapidated parts of the dwelling.
All other points are as stated above.
A bhikṣu must not perform labor for a layperson;
if he does so according to whatever task is assigned, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
The Text for the *Jñapti-karman* on Receiving the [Rainy Season] Robe: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
There is the bhikṣu so-and-so."

Regarding the practice of receiving the seven-day, fifteen-day, or one-month [leave]: if one must go outside the boundary for the purpose of being summoned, or due to circumstances such as medical treatment by the Triple Gem, one should state, "I shall go outside the boundary for one month."
Having thus performed the appropriate formal act for each case, he returns to this community to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
He makes the following announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen.

The bhikṣu [Name] has received the 'seven-day-at-most' authorization (*saptarātrātikrāntika-vidhi*)—whether for fifteen days, one day, or as it should be said, for one month—and shall go outside the boundary."
For the purpose of summoning [the Sangha] for the sake of the Triple Gem, medical treatment,
or other such occasions, [the monks] shall each attend to their respective duties and return here to observe the rains retreat. Which elders consent?

The Saṃgha listens: Let the bhikṣu [Name] receive the *saptāha-aticāra* (the rule for exceeding seven days) for a period of fifteen days or one month, as appropriate, to go outside the boundary for the purpose of being summoned, or for other reasons;
let those who will return here to observe the rains retreat remain silent.
Whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has approved granting the *saptāha-vidhi* (the seven-day rule), or the fifteen-day or one-month rule as appropriate, to the bhikṣu [Name] to go outside the boundary.
For the purpose of summoning [the absent monks], having returned here from wherever they were called according to the circumstances, the rains retreat has been completed.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent,
this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the formal reception of the seven-day rule through face-to-face declaration (*pratyekam-śiras*), this Vinaya contains a provision permitting the reception of the seven-day period;
thus the Vinaya states:
"I authorize the reception [of the *saptāha*], yet there is no specific ritual for its reception."
It should be understood that for those who receive the Dharma as practiced by both the ancients and the moderns,
it is established solely through the meaning of the *karmavācanā* formulas.
If one receives the seven-day [passage], one obtains only six nights.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "And on the seventh day, he returns.
The text says: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu [name], receive the seven-day rule."
Having gone outside the boundary for a certain matter,
I shall return here to observe the rains retreat.

"I announce to the Venerable Ones for their knowledge: [this is] the third formal declaration of the mind-intention method for receiving the seven-day *saptāha* [period]. This Vinaya contains no text permitting the mind-intention method for receiving [the *saptāha*];
however, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it permits five types of persons, such as those living alone.
Among the seven types of mental reflections, "receiving for seven days" is one such number.
One should say: "I, the bhikṣu [name], receive the seven-day rule to go outside the boundary."

For the sake of a certain matter, one returns to this community to observe the rains retreat; thus it is said three times. Regarding the method for declaring one's consent (*chanda*), there are four types.

The first is the declaration of one's own consent, which means that having gone into the midst of the Saṃgha oneself and made the declaration, one then departs. As the text says: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen."

I, the bhikṣu [Name], for the sake of a certain matter, regarding a formal monastic procedure (*dharmika saṃghakārya*), grant my consent and purity; this is declared once, with the second and third being spoken for others. The text says: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen."
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. Due to a certain matter concerning a certain bhikṣu named so-and-so, I have received his consent for purity (*kāyacitta-śuddhi*).

Regarding this formal act of the Saṃgha, I declare the consent for purity once; three times I do so for myself and for others—meaning that while I have my own business, I have further received the consent of others to be declared within the Saṃgha."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], for the sake of such-and-such a matter,
have received that person's consent for purity. I,
the bhikṣu [Name], for the sake of such-and-such a matter...
Both he and I shall each act according to the Dharma.

Regarding the granting of consent (*chanda*) and purity (*śuddhi*) for monastic affairs: it is said that one grants consent and purity by making a single formal declaration (*ekavācika*) through four turns of the procedure. As for "granting consent and purity," this refers to when, having already received the consent of another, one suddenly encounters a personal circumstance.
One must not go into the midst of the Saṃgha;
rather, one should approach another bhikṣu and state it clearly.
The text says: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], for the sake of such-and-such a matter..."
I accept that desire as pure. I,
the bhikṣu [name], for the sake of such-and-such a matter,
both he and I shall act in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding the matter of the Saṃgha, one who has received the *chanda* (consent) and the *pāriśuddhi* (purification) should go into the midst of the Saṃgha and state them directly as is customary.
As for the procedure for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) within the Saṃgha, it must be performed by at least five persons or more.
If even one person is missing, it is not accomplished.
Two persons should be appointed for the selection; those appointed must necessarily possess the five virtues:
being without attachment, without aversion, without fear, and without delusion.
Having understood this, one may perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) oneself or with others.
If there are five people, each may be appointed individually;
if there are six people, two may be appointed as a pair without fault.
The Text for the Ordination of One Possessing the Five Virtues: Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and willing, authorize the appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] as the person to receive the invitation to confession (*pravāraṇā*).
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to act as the recipient of the invitation to confess faults (*pravāraṇā*). Which elders consent?"
If the monk so-and-so, appointed by the Saṃgha to act as the recipient of the *pravāraṇā*, is in agreement, let him remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Sangha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the person to receive the *pravāraṇā*;
because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
[Regarding] the five virtuous qualities for the method of the Sangha’s *pravāraṇā* announcement: once the five virtuous ones have been appointed, they proceed as follows.
Having already proceeded to the seat of the senior elder and taken one's place, the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) is made as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
Today is the fifteenth day of the waxing moon; the community of monks shall perform the *pravāraṇā*."
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience:
the Saṃgha shall perform the *pravāraṇā* in harmony.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). If it is the dark fortnight, refer to it accordingly.
After announcing the date and other such details in this manner,
one should then address the assembly, saying:
"The members of the Saṃgha should each bare the right shoulder."
First, one should approach the grass seat, kneel with the right knee on the ground,
and join the palms to receive the *pravāraṇā* according to the Dharma.
Then, two individuals possessing the five virtues shall take turns kneeling to receive the *pravāraṇā*.
One must not stand while waiting.
The Text for the Individual *Pravāraṇā* of the Saṃgha: "Venerable One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
Today, the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], also perform the invitation to admonition (*pravāraṇā*).
If there be any offense seen, heard, or suspected,
may the virtuous elders, out of compassion, speak to me.

If I see my own transgressions, I shall confess them according to the Dharma three times. If there are two, three, or four persons, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) together with one another.
The text says: "O three elders, please attend to me with a single mind."
"Today the Saṃgha observes the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*).
I, the bhikṣu [Name], also observe the invitation for self-examination and am pure. (This is said three times. The response is: "So be it.
The procedure for others is likewise; for a single person, it is performed through mental reflection.

Regarding the procedure for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish), with the exception of the single phrase "Venerable Elder, please attend to me with one mind," everything else is identical to the rules for the light belongings of a deceased bhikṣu; first, have the bhikṣu who attended the deceased hold the light belongings of the deceased.
One should relinquish it within the Saṃgha.
The text says: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has passed away at this residence. If he died elsewhere, one should say, "at that residence. [Regarding] whatever robes or non-robes belonged to him...
After the formal announcement has been made three times for distribution among the monks present, one should say in summary:
"I, the bhikṣu [Name], hold these robes and articles and relinquish them to [Name]."
When one who knows the Vinaya has thus relinquished [the robe], one should first ask: "Is there a nurse? If he says:
If there are such persons, one should ask:
"Does anyone individually owe the deceased's property to the Three Jewels?
Or does the deceased owe property to anyone individually belonging to the Three Jewels?"
If it is claimed that [the object] exists, it should be subject to verification and restitution;
only then may the ritual procedure be performed.
The protocol for performing this ritual must establish four fixed standards.
First, whether they arise together or do not arise together;
second, whether the entrustment is accomplished or not;
third, the detailed analysis of light and heavy offenses.
The fourth, "Rewarding Labor," subsumes the preceding three.
According to the categories of matters, there are somewhat more [instances]; consult the extensive version for details.
To violate the names is what is forbidden.
There is no need for excessive citation.
Fourth, regarding the matter of distributing rewards, it must be fully set forth.

As for the method of rewarding labor: in establishing a system for rewarding merit, one must fully detail the services rendered and accord with the prescribed rites; only then will the procedure be properly accomplished.
That is to say, one who is endowed with the five virtues may receive [the precepts]; this person lacks them.
One who does not conform to the five virtues is ineligible.
1. To know what the patient may or may not eat, and to provide it accordingly;
2. Not to defile oneself with excrement, urine, saliva, or vomit;
3. To be able to manage the patient’s medicine and provisions with a sense of thorough dedication.
Regarding the four [qualities], those who possess a compassionate heart should not lack them; as for whether such a person possesses them or not—
if it is said they do— have them counted so that one may know with certainty that they are complete.
Thereafter, perform the ritual procedures for requesting permission and selecting the assembly as is customary.
The *karmavācanā* for rewarding labor is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has passed away at this residence—or if it was elsewhere, one should say 'at that residence. Whatever robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, cloth-bag, or alms-bowl he possessed among these six articles, should [be dealt with]."
Whatever is currently present shall be distributed among the *saṃgha* before their eyes.
If the time is right for the *saṃgha*, may the *saṃgha* grant its consent and listen:
the *saṃgha* now bestows [this] upon the monk so-and-so, who is tending to the sick.
The announcement is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
The bhikṣu [Name], having passed away at this residence, possesses these items:
robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing bag."
The property present before the Saṃgha should be divided;
it is now given to the bhikṣu [Name], the attendant for the sick.
Which elders consent?
The Sangha grants robe-cloths, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing-bag to monk so-and-so, the attendant for the sick. Those who consent remain silent;
those who do not consent speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented;
it has finished granting the robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing-bag container to the monk so-and-so, who is tending to the sick.
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent.
This matter is thus maintained; the procedure for rewarding labor being concluded, the distribution of robes follows next.
However, according to the explicit texts of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, one must first appoint a single person endowed with five virtues.

The one who distributes the robes is defined as one who is without attachment, without aversion, without fear, and without delusion; one who knows what has been distributed and what remains undistributed;

and one who, having waited for the appropriate time, price, color, and differences in quality, and having identified the recipients, then proceeds to carry out the method of distribution. Some establish three requirements for such a person.
This textual passage is unclear.
Furthermore, regarding the current practice where one frequently performs the hundred-and-twelfth dharma,
it is treated as being subsumed within the divisions.
I fear it is difficult;
by comparison, there are many deficiencies.
This is the current standard for the practice of our school.
It is absolutely necessary to appoint a person to administer the rules.
The inquiries regarding harmony and so forth are as above.
The *karmavācanā* for appointing a person to distribute robes: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I now appoint the bhikṣu [Name] as the distributor of robes for the Saṃgha.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Venerable Saṃgha, please listen.
Now, the monk so-and-so is appointed by the Saṃgha to act as the distributor of robes.
Those elders who consent to the appointment of the monk so-and-so as the distributor of robes should remain silent.
"Whoever does not approve, let them speak; the Sangha has approved.
The appointment of the monk [Name] as the distributor of robes for the Sangha is concluded.
Because the Sangha approves by remaining silent."
This matter is to be upheld in this manner.
*The Ritual Text for the Distribution of Light Valuables*: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
If the bhikṣu [Name] has passed away at this residence, or has died elsewhere, it is said that whatever robes or non-robes belong to that residence shall be divided among the present Saṃgha."
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha listen with patience.
The Sangha now bestows [this] upon the monk so-and-so; that monk shall return it to the Sangha.
This is the motion. Venerable Sangha, please listen.
A certain bhikṣu has passed away at this residence.
Whatever robes or non-robes he possessed should be divided by the present Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now bestows [these] upon the bhikṣu [Name]. The bhikṣu [Name].
It shall be returned to the Saṃgha. Which elders consent?
A certain bhikṣu has passed away at this residence.
If there are robes that are not [proper] robes, they should be divided among the present Saṃgha.
If you agree that the Saṃgha shall now give these to the bhikṣu so-and-so,
and that the bhikṣu so-and-so shall return them to the Saṃgha, remain silent.
Whoever does not approve, let them speak; the Saṃgha approves and maintains this.
These robes and articles are given to the bhikṣu [Name] and the bhikṣu [Name];
they shall be returned to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha approves, as it is silent.
This matter is to be maintained as follows: Regarding the method for dividing the belongings of a deceased bhikṣu, one should say: "Venerable sirs, please attend to me with one mind.
A bhikṣu named so-and-so has passed away at this residence."
Whatever robes there may be that are not currently being used as robes should be divided among the present Sangha;
since there is no Sangha here,
these robes belong to us.
"This is our share" should be recited three times.

Once one person has spoken, the other two need not speak as well. Regarding the method for distributing the property of a deceased bhikṣu through mental reflection, it should be said: "Bhikṣu so-and-so has passed away at this residence."
If there are robes or what are not robes,
the present Saṃgha should divide them here;
where there is no Saṃgha, these robes belong to me.
I should employ a single exposition.
Regarding the text for receiving and maintaining the three robes (*tricīvara*), the text on the three robes as the moral path of the Three Holy Jewels, and the text on reverence—
these are analogous to the names and essences of Buddha-stūpas, which manifest unprecedented dharmas.
The power [of this teaching] subdues the ninety-six paths; those who practice it and observe the precepts must follow the Noble Dharma.

Whether one has not yet received the robes or is without robes, both other schools and our own school universally require that they be accepted. May you respectfully uphold the instructions of the Compassionate One within your hearts.
The Text for Receiving the Saṃghāṭī: "Venerable Sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], this robe is a fifteen-panel saṃghāṭī."
Having received the three long and one short cut-and-sewn robes (*khaṇḍa-cīvara*), he maintained them; when asked about this, he replied, "It may be so," and all other cases were treated accordingly.
Only regarding the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) as determined by the teachings, there are three grades and nine categories.
The ninth and thirteenth articles both state:
"two long, one short. The fifteenth, seventeenth, and nineteenth all state:
"three long, one short."
The twenty-first, twenty-third, and twenty-fifth [verses] all state:
"four long and one short.
When performing the ritual procedure, one should understand this according to the standard measurements.
The Text for Receiving the Seven-Striped Robe: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [name], this *uttarāsaṅga* robe consisting of seven strips..."
The Text for Receiving the Five-Striped *Antarvāsa* (Inner Robe) Made from Two Long and One Short Cut-and-Sewn Cloths: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am receiving this five-striped *antarvāsa* robe."
The Text for Receiving One Long and One Short Patchwork Robe and for Renouncing the Three Robes after Reciting Them Three Times: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have this saṃghāṭī as my third robe."
I have previously received and maintained several [robes].
Now, for the purpose of replacement, I relinquish them by reciting this three times.
The same applies to the remaining two robes.

If one follows the procedure for relinquishing [the robes], and the three robes are in a different location such that one cannot assemble with them by nightfall, one should face a single bhikṣu and perform the ritual of relinquishment from a distance, saying: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], this saṃghāṭī is my third robe, which I have formally accepted and maintained as my basic requisite.
Now, because one cannot attend the assembly, one relinquishes the three [modes of speech]; the relinquishment of the other two robes is to be conducted according to this standard.
If there is no bhikṣu present, one should perform mental recollection and verbal declaration;
according to this, one should omit everything except the single phrase: "Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind."
All else is as above.
The Text for Receiving and Maintaining the *Naiṣīdana* (Sitting Mat): "Venerable Sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name],..."
This *niṣīdana* should be made according to the prescribed measurements; now I accept it—this is said three times.
The formula for relinquishing: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind."
I, Bhikṣu [Name], this niṣīdana has been made to the proper measure;
having previously accepted and maintained it, I now relinquish it— thus three times.
Text for Receiving and Holding the Alms Bowl: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu [name], shall receive this pātra bowl, which is of the proper measure."
Because it is commonly practiced, it is explained in three ways.
Regarding the method for the successive purification of the gift (*pariśuddha-dāna*), one should invite a monk who is learned, observant of the precepts, virtuous, and renowned.
If he is a senior elder, one should prostrate at his feet, kneel with the right knee on the ground, and join the palms in invitation.
If it is a minor offense, the prostration at the feet is omitted;
the Bhikṣuṇī, Śikṣamāṇā, Śrāmaṇera, and Śrāmaṇerī precepts may all be received in this manner.
If it is for a Bhikṣu, one should say: "Venerable Sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind."
I, the bhikṣu [Name],
now request the Venerable One to act as the intermediary purifier for robes, medicine, and the alms bowl.
May the Venerable One act as my intermediary purifier for robes, medicine, and the alms bowl.
Recite this three times out of compassion.
From this point forward, one should declare the purity (*śuddhi*) in the presence of a single bhikṣu;
however, one must not declare the purity in the presence of the donor.
Furthermore, one must not speak so as to make it known.
The text for the declaration of purity (*śuddhi-ārocana*): "Venerable sir, attend to me for a moment. I, the bhikṣu [name],..."
"I have this extra robe which has not yet been purified.
Now, for the sake of the 'successive purification' (saṃvartanīya-viśuddhi), I give it to you, Venerable Sir; having spoken thus, you should hand it over to that bhikṣu."
Having received it, that bhikṣu should say to him: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
Venerable sir, you have this long robe which has not yet been purified;
for the sake of mutual purification, I request that you give it to me."
I now accept it; having accepted it, I shall ask him: "Who is your donor? He should reply: "So-and-so. The recipient should speak thus: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind."
"Elder, you possess this extra robe which has not yet been formally dedicated (*apariṇata*).
For the sake of mutual dedication (*parivartaka-pariṇāma*), you have given it to me; I now accept it."
The Elder says of himself:
"The donor is such-and-such a person;
I am holding this object to bestow it upon such-and-such a person."
"This robe already belongs to so-and-so;
Venerable One, please guard it for him.
It may be used as one pleases. (Recite this once.)
The Ritual for Receiving Non-Timely Beverages: "Venerable Sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu [name], now, for the cause and condition of thirst..."
These are pomegranate juice, various fruit juices, and so forth; they are designated as "desirable" (*kāma*) because they may be consumed outside of the proper time (*akāla*).
Now, one receives [the permission for] these other juices from a virtuous elder by reciting the formula three times, following this same principle.
The Text for Receiving Seven-Day Medicine: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [name], for the sake of a certain illness..."
This ghee-oil is a seven-day medicine;
because it is intended to be kept and consumed for seven days,
I now receive it from the Venerable One, reciting the formula three times.
The Text on Receiving Medicinal Substances for Treatment: Venerable One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], now, for the sake of a certain illness, receive as medicinal substances for my lifetime these ginger, pepper, and other items—hot or cold—as appropriate to my condition.

Because one desires to stay overnight and consume it for a long duration, one now receives [the permission] from the Venerable One by reciting the formula three times; he replies accordingly. Furthermore, there are four types of this medicine:

namely, that which is permitted at the proper time (*kāla*), that which is permitted outside the proper time (*akāla*), that which lasts for seven days (*saptāha*), and that which lasts for as long as life endures (*yāvajjīva*).
If the four medicines are mixed together, one should take them according to whichever is strongest.
Once taken, do not allow anyone who has not received full ordination (*upasampadā*) to touch them.
Within the prescribed limit, they may be taken at all times, day and night, without interruption.
If one consumes [these] after a disease has been cured, or if one consumes them when not ill,
one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Furthermore, there are foolish elders in the world who, during improper times,
drink milk, curd, bean soup, or jujube decoction.
Or [they may eat] rice gruel and the like,
as well as various fruits such as pomegranate, pear, crab-apple, grape, and red crab-apple;
upon obtaining them, they chew them and swallow the juice.
To say that the teaching permits [the consumption of] fermented liquids is truly a matter of great regret.
Regarding fruits and the like used to make gruel,
the Noble One commanded that they be pounded, pressed, and divided.
Remove the dregs from the liquid and retain the juice;
take it and clarify it,
then add and mix it with pure water.
This would destroy its original flavor.
Thus, one must act in accordance with the Dharma before one may begin to permit [the practice].
To allow the mind to flow ahead [of the ritual] is truly an act of irreverence and arrogance.
Furthermore, one may grind parched flour, barley meal, and various medicines such as *gu-pra-ja* together;
or, one may mix sesame powder with ghee, honey, and other substances to prepare it as a medicine for use outside of the prescribed mealtime (*akālabhojana*).
In such cases as these, for whatever one eats, every swallow constitutes an offense of *thullaccaya*.
This is merely the result of foolish, ruinous, and deluded thoughts leading to indiscriminate practice.
Those who intend to give rise to the precepts and preserve the Path should be cautious regarding this.

Regarding the method for repentance of the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture): while "forfeiture" specifically refers to the thirty [rules], the meaning of "repentance" applies generally to all other categories of offenses (*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, etc.).

When one intends to forfeit a robe, one should announce the intention and reflect; all robes corresponding to the transgressions committed should be gathered together. Once they have been thus assembled, one should first reproach one's own mind and perform the confession.
Excluding the eight categories of *dukkaṭa* offenses, it is not necessarily the case that all individuals possess all eight;
now, based on the meaning of the text, their characteristics shall be set forth. One should personally reflect upon one’s own mind and examine them carefully according to the text.
Regarding the statement "one who knows for oneself that [an offense] exists" as the heading for the confession, the phrase "eight categories" refers to:
first, having committed a fundamental *pārājika* offense,
one recognizes the transgression and forms the intention to conceal it.
If one stays overnight within the same boundary as pure bhikṣus, one commits one grade of *duṣkṛta* for concealment (*paryuṣita*).

Having stayed for a second night, one further commits a successive grade of *duṣkṛta* for concealment; these two grades of offense arise from the root *pāyattika* offense. If one wears a *naiḥsargika* robe that has not been relinquished, [the following applies].
If one wears each of these impure robes, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); this constitutes the root offense.
Furthermore, if one recalls knowing this offense and harbors a mind of concealment, and stays overnight together with pure monks, one commits a *dukkaṭa* of concealment.

After the second night has passed, one further commits the *duṣkṛta* offense of concealing [the transgression] as it spreads; this constitutes the application of the three grades. Thus, the various offenses listed above are collectively recalled and recognized.

If one commits an offense and conceals it with a mind of concealment, and after the Sangha has recited the Prātimokṣa three times during the confession of offenses, one remains silent, this constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta* for lying; this is the root offense. Furthermore, if one maintains a mind of concealment regarding this offense for even a single night, [it becomes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*].
Concealing [the offense] constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
Furthermore, if one maintains a concealing mind toward these two categories for more than one night, [it becomes a *sthūlātyaya*].

Furthermore, one commits a *duṣkṛta* for concealing [the offense] as it successively arises; these constitute the three categories of silent falsehood. These eight categories are all to be expiated through mental remorse (*cittavipratisāra*). The procedure for performing the confession is as follows: one should bare the right shoulder.
With a sincere heart, prostrate to the Buddhas of the ten directions,
generating a sense of profound reverence as if they were standing before one's eyes.
Deeply reproach oneself for having lacked a sense of shame and remorse.

Because they have committed offenses by showing contempt for the sublime teachings, the karmic results will ripen in the three periods of time; certain that they must undergo this, they shed copious tears of thought.
Then, with voices choked by bitter sorrow, they give rise to a sense of profound shame.

Then, perform the ritual procedure as follows: "I, the bhikṣu [name], have intentionally kept many extra robes (*atirekacīvara*). If I recall their number, I shall declare the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* according to that number.

In this regard, if one wears or uses an impure robe, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one does not recall the number, or recalls the number and declares it accordingly—the same applies to all subsequent cases—if one conceals this offense with a hidden mind, it is a *pāyattika* for concealment; if one does not recall the number, the same applies.
Furthermore, there are offenses of *duṣkṛta* for concealing [the offense] as it was committed or as it subsequently developed, which cannot be counted;
there are offenses of *duṣkṛta* for committing a lie by remaining silent during the *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts when one has committed an offense, which cannot be counted;
and among these, there are offenses of *duṣkṛta* for concealing [the offense], which cannot be counted.
Furthermore, regarding the *duṣkṛta* offenses committed through successive concealment, which I do not recall the number of, I now confess and repent before all the Buddhas.
I dare not conceal them; through repentance, I shall immediately find peace and happiness.
One finds no peace or joy without repentance;
by recollecting the offense and disclosing it,
one knows it and does not conceal it.
I only pray that all Buddhas will take note of me: my body of pure precepts is complete and I have maintained the pure *poṣadha*.

I now reproach myself and give rise to a mind of weary detachment. First, I confess the one *duṣkṛta* of intentional lying; second, I confess the two fundamental *duṣkṛtas* of using [a robe] while attached to it and concealing [an offense], following the previous procedure by calling out their names. It should be known that for the remaining sections of the *skandhas*, there are five grades of *duṣkṛtas*; however, if the *poṣadha* recitation has not been performed, there are only two grades.

It should be understood that the rules for the method of confession are all identical to the aforementioned procedures; the only difference lies in the formal document (nṛpa) which specifies each individual offense. Regarding the text on the forfeiture of property:
whenever one intends to perform the rite of relinquishing an article subject to forfeiture, it must be done in accordance with the two boundaries (sīmā).
Because all the monks within the boundary must assemble together,
the Vinaya states:
"Whether it be the Saṃgha, a large group of people, or a single individual."
All must be gathered together; one may not discard them in a separate assembly.
If discarded otherwise, the discarding is invalid and one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This exception does not apply to the two types of precious items—thread and cloth—which are permitted to be discarded in a separate assembly; for all others, this is not allowed.
Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept many extra robes; knowing their number, I must state it according to that actual count, as they have exceeded ten days.

One commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). Now, holding these robes and garments, one relinquishes them to a Venerable One with a single recitation; the other replies, "So be it," and then accepts them.

Thus, by staying overnight separated from the three robes—whether one, two, or three of them—one commits an offense involving forfeiture according to the specific name [of the robe]. By buying and selling and obtaining wealth in various quantities, one commits numerous offenses involving forfeiture.

Whether one begs for several garments from a householder who is not a relative and thus commits an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya), or even up to the case of diverting the property of the Saṅgha—
one should address each according to its specific name.
It should be understood that the text for requesting the presiding master of confession should be recited softly before a single pure bhikṣu.
Regarding the absence of further offenses,
the Vinaya states:
"One should proceed to a place of purity."
Why must this be so? If that person commits an offense, they immediately become bound by themselves;
being already bound, how can they rescue others?
The text says: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], now request the Venerable sir to act as the presiding master for the confession of a pāyattika offense."
"I pray that the Venerable One will act as my preceptor for the confession of a *pāyattika* offense.
Out of compassion, [this is] stated three times. He replies, "So be it.
To clearly explain the ritual for confession, the text says: "Venerable One, with a single mind..."
I, the bhikṣu [name], intentionally kept many long pieces of cloth, numbering so-and-so, exceeding ten days, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
These robes have now been relinquished to the Venerable One, or relinquished to another person.

One should say: "I have already relinquished it to another person. In this case, regarding the root *pāyattika* offense, if the number is not remembered but can be known to be small, one should state it accordingly based on that estimation.
Just as with the three robes (*tricīvara*),
one must always refer to them by their specific number and may not call them "many";
for after a long period of time, they may be worn out through use.
Each has committed a fundamental *pāyattika* offense, and the number is not remembered.
If the property were all present, this statement would not be necessary; now, I confess and repent before the Venerable One.
Not daring to conceal them, one repents and immediately attains peace and happiness;
without repentance, there is no peace or happiness.
One should mindfully recall the transgressions and disclose them.
Knowing this, I do not dare to conceal it.
I pray that the Venerable One will bear witness that my body of pure precepts is complete and that my *poṣadha* is pure.

(This is said three times. The presiding master of the confession should say to him: "Elder, do you recognize the characteristics of this offense? He should reply: "I recognize them. The presiding master should further say: "You must reproach your own mind and give rise to deep weariness and detachment."

The response was, "So be it. The junior [monk] said, "I shall receive this upon my head. Having finished reciting this in relation to the *atireka-cīvara* (extra robe), the other precepts and so forth may be understood by analogy.

Next, the method for returning property is explained: among the thirty precepts, there are five rules in total concerning the *atireka-cīvara*, the one-day robe (*ekarātra-cīvara*), the extra bowl (*atireka-pātra*), the seven-day medicine, and the medicine received after the period of urgent dispensation has passed.
In all cases, one must return [the precepts] after spending the night;
however, for the remaining precepts and so forth, one may return them immediately while still seated.
If, however, one renounces a category of precepts common to these five precepts, it is also permissible to follow the rule of returning them after spending the night.
Except for the three robes and the six-year bedding, which must be relinquished; for these, one need not wait overnight, but may return them immediately upon sitting down.
If one borrows another's three robes and undergoes the ritual of destruction, the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) is successfully established.
If one stays apart [from one's robe] for a night, the formal undertaking is lost and one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
One should know that while one must repent for the offense, it is improper to discard the robe as it is the property of another.
Regarding the general procedure for the method of confessing offenses according to the five categories of transgressions, the Buddha said:
"One should go before a pure bhikṣu, fully maintain the dignified deportment, and state the name of the offense committed.
One should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*) as follows: 'Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.'"
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense.
I now disclose it before the Venerable One.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual confession according to the Dharma, reciting it three times.
Regarding the method for disclosing doubtful offenses, the meaning applies generally to the five categories of the Vinaya;
it states that when there is doubt regarding the commission of an offense:
[The instructor] presses [the candidate] to speak the words of the Buddha.
Having confessed, they hear the meaning of the precepts according to the Dharma, which says: "Venerable Sir, please bear it in mind:
I, the bhikṣu [Name],..."
"I have a doubt regarding a certain offense;
I now disclose it before you, Venerable Sir.
I shall do so again when I am free from doubt."
Having performed the confession according to the Dharma three times, he should say, "So be it.

Once he has finished eating, he should perform the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rite for leftover food) and, holding the food, should speak thus to a monk who has not yet finished his meal: "Venerable sir..."
"I have already finished my meal.
Venerable sir, please know this and observe this.
Having said this, he should perform the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rite of leftover food) and then take a small amount of it and eat.
He said, "I have finished eating;
you take this food and eat it."
Request for Dependence: Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], now request the Venerable One to be my dependence-ācārya.
"I pray that the Venerable One will act as my *niśraya-ācārya*.
Relying upon the Venerable One, I shall abide in accordance with the Dharma.
Out of compassion, [the candidate] should say this three times, and the other should respond: "So be it."
"It may be so. Either he says, "I grant you the dependence," or he says,
"Do not be negligent"— uttering one of these three phrases.
There is no need to explain all of this in detail.
Before receiving the invitation for a meal, or after the meal, when entering a village, the formula for entrustment is as follows: "Venerable One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], having previously accepted an invitation from [Name],
now have a certain business and wish to enter the village of [Place Name] and go to the house of [Name].
Having informed the Venerable One that the entrustment has been performed,
if one goes elsewhere or returns midway,
the previous procedure is lost in both cases.
If one wishes to go, one should perform the ritual procedure again.
The formal announcement for entering a village at an improper time: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [name],..."
"One should not enter a certain village or go to a certain house at an improper time;
one must inform a venerable elder so that he may know of it.
He replied: "If there is an invitation or summons, it is unnecessary to make such an announcement."
The Method for Performing the Six Recollections (Ṣaḍ-anusmṛti): First Recollection:
Knowing the length of the month and whether it is a full or new moon. If it is before the fifteenth day of a full moon month, one should say: "This is a full moon month."
From the first day up to the fifteenth day,
one refers to them by their respective names.
From the sixteenth day onwards, they are all called the "dark fortnight" (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
One should say: "This month is a large dark fortnight," followed by the first day up to the fifteenth day as appropriate;
if the month is small, one should say: "This month is a small [fortnight]."
The ritual procedure is according to the preceding [instructions]. If following the *Cīvaravastu*,
it is always during the waxing moon.
The dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) is designated according to its length.
Now, since one wishes to understand that in this region the lunar days for both the monastic and lay communities differ from those of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*,
we shall follow the method established in the Western Land (India).
However, one may simply use the term "month" in its general sense according to the meaning,
while further specifying the distinctions of the śramaṇa’s days, months, waxing, and waning phases.
This is the second reflection.
Regarding the place of eating: if one habitually begs for food, one should say, "I always beg for food.
If one eats what has already been prepared, one should say, "I am eating what has already been prepared.
If one eats the food of the Sangha, one should say, "I am eating the food of the Sangha."
If there is no fixed location for the meal, one should say, "I request food from below my back.
If there is only a single invitation, one may mentally notify oneself.
If there are many places of invitation and one cannot personally notify them all, [one should proceed accordingly].
The person who first delivers the invitation may respond on behalf of themselves; for all others, the response should be sent by proxy.
The bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras at the place where the invitation is delivered are both permitted to respond.
The ritual procedure states: "Venerable [Name],
a donor has invited me for the five kinds of formal meals."
I have circumstances that prevent me from going;
I now give this to you as an offering.
If there is no one else who can receive it, [take it].
Following the *Mahāsāṃghika* and *Pañcavargika* Vinayas, one should perform the mental relinquishment as follows: "I, the bhikṣu [Name],
this morning received five kinds of formal meals from a donor."
"I transfer this gift to the bhikṣu [Name].
The donor is not bound to me; I shall eat it. If one turns away from the previous house and heads toward the subsequent house, one should recite this three times.
Behind the back, one should recite it once while facing the previous house.
The third mindfulness:
knowing the time of receiving the precepts, one should state the frequency of the thought, "On such a year, such a month, such a day, and at such a time,
I received full ordination."
A piece of wood one chi long has no shadow at certain times;
if there is a shadow, it corresponds to its length, whether much or little.
This is the fourth reflection.
Having ascertained whether the robes and bowl have been purified,
if one does not possess the three robes, one should resolve to obtain them;
if one possesses them, one should resolve to maintain them.
If one possesses surplus wealth, one should maintain the mindfulness of its purification (*śuddhi*).
If a robe is complete or incomplete, one should follow the rule of not being mindful of its completeness.
If there is surplus clothing, whether it has been purified or not, one should maintain the mindfulness that it shall be purified.
If one possesses both robes and bowl, and has already accepted extra wealth that has been purified, one should say: "I possess the three robes and bowl and maintain them;
all extra robes have been declared as purified.
This is the fifth mindfulness.
Knowing whether food is shared or separate, one should say: "I rely on communal food, not on food taken separately.
This is the sixth mindfulness.
Knowing whether one is ill or not ill.
If one has an illness, one should say: "I now have an illness;
I shall attend to its treatment. If one is without illness, one simply says: [as appropriate].
This morning I am free from illness and am practicing the Path in accordance with the community.

Regarding the rules for receiving and keeping money and precious objects, as well as the method for purifying them: the arising of money and precious objects is a grave transgression and a great affliction on the Path.
When worldly customs are shallow and corrupt yet still prize lofty integrity,
how much more so for those who have left the household life to transcend the mundane? To suddenly begin storing up such things would cause one to fall far from the pure wind of their tradition.
Recently, I have visited your humble abode.
Admiring the Way, you have reached a level of understanding and should now lightly take up the vehicle.
Nevertheless, as one relies on conditions to sustain the Way, [you must remain diligent].

Regarding the two types of cultivated plants and the five kinds of seeds: first, root-seeds, such as ginger and all those propagated from branches; second, branch-seeds, such as willows and all those propagated from branches; third, joint-seeds, such as smartweed and all those produced from joints; fourth, bulb-seeds, such as sugarcane and lotus roots; fifth, seed-seeds, namely the seventeen grains and all other varieties of seeds. Among these, for those that are roots, branches, or joints, they are purified by cutting them in half with a knife.
Among the various types of joints, one should remove the nodes and clean away the eyes;

First, pitted fruits (*kapittha-phala*), such as dates, apricots, and the like; second, skin-fruits (*tvaṅ-mukha-phala*), such as peaches, plums, pears, nectarines, and so forth; third, shell-fruits (*kaṭāha-phala*), namely coconuts, walnuts, chestnuts, pomegranates, and the like; fourth, husked-fruits (*tuṣa-phala*), such as fragrant grasses, sesame, linseed, and so forth; fifth, pod-fruits (*kośa-phala*), such as large and small beans, legumes, and the like. There should first be five dharmas.

First, one should cultivate loving-kindness with a compassionate heart toward all beings, thereby distancing oneself from the defilement of anger and benefiting both self and others. Second, one should humble oneself, maintaining a lowly mind and a submissive disposition like that of one wiping away dust.
One should subdue arrogance;
one should yield what is right to others and take blame upon oneself. Third, one should properly know how to sit and rise:
if one sees a senior elder (sthavira), one should not remain seated.
If one sees those of lower rank, one should not rise to greet them; knowing well one’s own station, one should act with propriety in both motion and stillness.

Free from the flattery and arrogance of the common folk, one should accord with the mind of the Noble Ones. Fourth, when entering the midst of the Saṃgha, one should not engage in miscellaneous talk or discuss worldly matters.
If one preaches the Dharma oneself,
